newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-SAMPRAS BLAMES SLOW BALLS FOR INJURIES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS BLAMES SLOW BALLS FOR INJURIES.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras blamed the tennis balls he used to cruise into the second round of the Australian Open on Tuesday for causing an increased risk of injuries.
The American was unhappy about the softness of the balls at Melbourne Park after dispatching Romanian qualifier Dinu Pescariu 6-2 6-4 6-2 in a ritual slaughter lasting 99 minutes on centre court.
Sampras, who was prone to arm injuries earlier in his career, echoed the complaints of ousted Australian Open champion Boris Becker.
Becker said after his shock first round exit to Spaniard Carlos Moya on Monday that softer balls were responsible for an increase in wrist and elbow injuries.
"I happen to agree with him," said Sampras, who described the heavier balls for the Australian Open as the slowest he had experienced on tour.
"My arm has been feeling just a little bit heavy over the past three or four days and I think it's because of the balls."

But tournament director Paul McNamee called a hastily-arranged media conference to deny the claim that the balls were slower than last year. He said testing by the manufacturer, Slazenger, showed they were as hard as those used in 1996 without player complaints.
"I have been playing the game for a lot of years and I can tell the balls are different," said Sampras, who is chasing his second Australian Open to add to his 1994 triumph.

"It (the slowness of the balls) does not help you to serve and volley but it gives you more time to make a return of serve. It is difficult to put the ball away, and difficult to be aggressive," he said.
Becker said in his post-match media conference: "For the hitters, it's a real killer," adding the arm takes a greater strain because the players are forced to hit the ball harder.
Sampras said he puts ice on his arm after matches and practice sessions in a bid to avoid the injury problems that plagued his career several years ago.
Sampras will play another Romanian, Adrian Voinea, in the second round.
McNamee said the speed of the court and the hardness of the balls had not been changed since last year.
"We were very happy with the situation last year and the last thing we wanted to do was change anything," McNamee said.
But McNamee, a former Australia Davis Cup player said tournament organisers would consider the players' complaints at the end of the two-week tournament.
